In 27 regions of the Russian Federation, the immunodeficiency virus is spreading among the entire population, not only risk groups, according to the latest Rospotrebnadzor data. People increasingly pass the virus to one another, often unaware they are infected.

In 27 Russian regions, there is a generalised HIV epidemic. This was reported by the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor. Scientists use this term for the stage when the human immunodeficiency virus spreads in the general population rather than only among risk groups.

In these regions, HIV is diagnosed in more than 1% of pregnant women. The situation is most serious in the Kemerovo, Irkutsk and Sverdlovsk regions.

And although, according to the Central Research Institute for the Prevention and Control of AIDS, 45,000 new HIV cases were detected in Russia in 2025, which is 13.4% lower than in 2024, last year a record was set for the number of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical institutions, according to statistics compiled by the specialist portal Medvestnik.

Experts record the highest level of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical facilities in 15 years

These are the highest figures in the past 15 years. Clusters of viral hepatitis C and mixed HIV plus hepatitis infections predominate, said Yelena Igonina, head of the Department for the Epidemiological Wellbeing of the Population at Rospotrebnadzor. In 2025, eight clusters of infection were recorded in healthcare facilities in Russia, with 104 patients infected.

According to Rospotrebnadzor, investigations continued in 2026 into 11 clusters of infection in the territory of ten regions of Russia, where the spread of HIV and hepatitis in medical organisations is suspected. In Moscow, an investigation is underway into a cluster in which 22 cases of viral hepatitis C have been identified.

One of the largest confirmed clusters in the past two years was the infection of 82 people in a sanatorium in Kabardino-Balkaria. While receiving medical care, 76 patients contracted viral hepatitis C and six were found to have mixed infections. In oncology hospitals in Kamchatka Territory and Buryatia, 147 and 42 patients, respectively, were infected with hepatitis. Another three hepatitis C clusters were identified in dialysis centres in the Samara and Kursk regions, where 26 people were affected.

Experts describe violations of sanitary and epidemiological rules as the main cause of the infections, including the use of single-use catheters or glucometers on several patients. In such situations, the source is usually patients with undiagnosed infections.

Yelena Igonina notes that these "systemic and gross violations" have become entrenched in today’s Russia. Although simultaneous testing for hepatitis C antibodies and RNA covers blood, component, organ and tissue donors well, testing for RNA among other categories that should be tested, namely dialysis, haematology and transplant patients, contacts in hepatitis clusters, children under one born to mothers with HIV and patients with immunodeficiency, is significantly lagging behind.

In addition, for the first time in six years, two cases of HIV infection via transfusion of blood components were identified in 2026, the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor added.

When hospitals receive large numbers of people with undiagnosed infections, international HIV consultant Aleksei Verter told Current Time, this means that "the infectious process in the country is latent, hidden" and a great many people do not know they are infected.

Despite lower mortality, the number of people living with HIV is rising

Despite a decline in HIV incidence and mortality in Russia in recent years, the number of people infected continues to grow, Medvestnik’s authors note. Statistics show that for each death there are one and a half new infections, that is, the number of people "living with HIV continues to grow constantly", explains Natalya Ladnaya.

The decline was preceded by a long period of rising incidence, but in the past three years rates of morbidity and mortality among people with HIV have been falling and, according to her preliminary data, this trend will continue in 2026. At the same time, the expert is convinced that there is no reason to rest on one’s laurels, since "the dynamics can change rapidly".

In recent years, the number of deaths from HIV in Russia has been between 30,000 and 34,000 per year. This is an extremely high figure, stresses the head of the research department for the prevention and control of AIDS at the Central Research Institute of Rospotrebnadzor. "Among all the countries in the world there are only 15 where more than 15,000 deaths of people with HIV are recorded, including Russia." "The highest HIV incidence rates per 100,000 population in the European region are in Russia, Ukraine and North Macedonia", says Central Research Institute of Epidemiology director and Rospotrebnadzor academician Vasily Akimkin.

HIV infection has become the leading cause of death among Russians of working age. Among men aged 40 to 49, more than 3% are affected by the virus, clarifies Natalya Ladnaya, while the average age of those infected in Russia has increased over the past 15 years from 32 to 44. It is also noteworthy that two-thirds of new HIV transmissions occur through heterosexual contact.

More than 1.232 million people with a confirmed HIV diagnosis now live in Russia, which is 0.8% of the country’s population, Akimkin adds. Rospotrebnadzor has warned that if current approaches to prevention and treatment remain unchanged, the number of people living with HIV in Russia could reach 1.47 million by 2030, according to the agency’s mathematical model. Under this scenario, the annual number of new cases will be between 31,000 and 51,000, and the number of deaths included in the model could rise to 51,000 a year, which is linked, among other things, to population ageing.

In the past seven years, the main causes of death among children with HIV have also changed. An increase in mortality in this group of patients was recorded in 2025 in all federal districts except the Central and Ural districts.

According to an analysis by several Russian media outlets, Rospotrebnadzor and the Health Ministry calculate figures differently. Rospotrebnadzor’s data are more complete, as they are based on laboratory notifications of every positive immunoblot. The Health Ministry’s data are based on the number of people who have been registered for regular follow-up care. As a result, the overall gap between the total number of people with a confirmed diagnosis, 1.23 million according to Rospotrebnadzor, and those actually under medical supervision, 846,500 according to the Health Ministry, amounts to 385,555 people.

600,000 infected people

Only half of people living with HIV in Russia had a suppressed viral load by the end of 2025, said Natalya Ladnaya at the conference "Epidemiological Surveillance of HIV Infection", as quoted by Medvestnik. In practice, this means that at least 600,000 people with HIV "continue to play an active part in transmitting the virus", the expert concludes.

Viral load suppression occurred last year in 77.9% of people with HIV who were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and "so far it has not been possible to exceed this level", she says, while WHO standards for keeping the epidemic under control are 95-95-95, that is, 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of them receive ART and 95% of those on therapy achieve suppression of HIV replication.

As for access to medical care for people living with HIV in Russia, 72% of those infected were under follow-up last year. Despite extensive HIV testing, which has increased by 75% over the past decade and reached 54 million tests last year, effectiveness is declining. In the view of the director of the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, approaches need to be adjusted by increasing the share of people at the highest risk of infection, who are insufficiently covered by testing. Their share has now almost halved, from 5.8% in 2014 to 3% in 2023.

But the effectiveness of the work is declining, meaning there are more tests, but testing is increasingly carried out among people with a lower probability of having HIV.

Chronic underfunding by the state

The fact that the burden of HIV infection is not decreasing even as incidence falls is reflected in healthcare spending, stresses Natalya Ladnaya. In 2025, spending related to HIV infection was estimated at 279 billion roubles.

In the expert’s view, there is no reason to expect the situation to change; on the contrary, the spread of the virus may intensify among traditionally vulnerable population groups and among people living in regions bordering Ukraine that are characterised by high levels of migration. According to Rospotrebnadzor, incidence and mortality may also rise in the Far Eastern, Southern and North Caucasian federal districts.

Bloggers have also spoken about the spread of viruses, including HIV, among those fighting against Ukraine. According to Anastasia Kashevarova, the Russian authorities should "seriously think about it, there is a threat of an epidemic of socially dangerous diseases", since hepatitis, HIV and tuberculosis are currently spreading in the army and to frontline regions, but "will then spread further into the interior of Russia".

The Insider previously reported that after Russia’s occupation of parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions, patients with HIV faced shortages of life-saving medicines. The Russian Health Ministry did not include them in centralised drug procurement, and some patients were given medicines past their expiry date.

According to observers, the fact that the healthcare budget is shrinking and all funds are going to the war helps explain, among other things, shortages of sterile consumables in state hospitals.

Other Russian media emphasise that most donors financing HIV prevention programmes for the general population and vulnerable groups have left Russia. The country itself does not adequately fund these projects, says Evgeny Pisemsky, editor-in-chief of the queer media outlet "Parni+", quoted by Current Time. With 45,000 new HIV cases detected in 2025, the draft Russian budget for 2027 provides for additional funding for medicines for only 30,000 new carriers of the virus.

From a shared table in economy to a double bed in first class, airlines are finding new ways to sell passengers more premium space and amenities as higher fuel costs squeeze profits.

Airlines are betting that more passengers will pay for an upgrade to their flight experience, with some carriers fitting roomier seats, bringing in Michelin-starred chefs to design onboard menus and also investing in elite airport lounges.

Some airlines envisage up to 70% of passengers paying for enhanced options, if not first-or business class. That shift could mean fewer standard economy seats on many flights.

The war in Iran has pushed up jet fuel costs, but airlines see premium travel as a way to boost profits over the long term.

Business class seats can each take up floor space equivalent to four basic-level seats, but can be priced five or six times higher, said Volodymyr Bilotka, a professor at Purdue University and a specialist in aviation economics.

"Airlines have traditionally been investing quite a lot into the premium offerings because the profit margins are significantly higher," Bilotka told the AFP news agency.

In the most recent quarter, American Airlines said premium revenue increased 18.5% year-over-year, four points better than the main cabin. American executives said the boost has been a bright spot in a travel market complicated by the jet fuel spike.

"Premium products generate roughly half of the company's ticket revenue on approximately 30% of seats today," American said.

Besides the traditional differentiation between the main cabin and business class, customers may now pay as much as $200 (€179) for more legroom or the ability to sit at the front of the plane and disembark first.

Premium's steady growth

Since 2020, the number of premium seats on US flights has risen 33%, more than double the growth of mainline seats, according to travel news site Skift.

United Airlines more than doubled its premium-seat capacity between 2015 and 2026, the airline told AFP, adding that it plans additional options.

Launching in 2027, United’s new “Relax Row” will allow passengers in economy class to turn a row of three seats on some wider Boeing planes into a couch they can sleep or lounge on after takeoff.

United has also unveiled its new Economy Plus option that allows customers to forgo having a passenger in the dreaded middle seat. It plans to begin this option on some flights at the end of 2026.

‘More premium experiences’

JetBlue announced the launch of BlueFirst, a new first-class service on domestic flights. "Customers are increasingly looking for more premium experiences," said JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty.

Meanwhile, Delta has invested in Delta One, a revamped luxury option, with premium wine, "top-of-the line" food like the Wagyu burger and larger screens for entertainment.

To assist with the menu, Delta partnered with Simon Hulstone, chef of Michelin-starred restaurant The Elephant in Torquay, UK, and Andrea Robinson, an award-winning sommelier.

The company plans the service for new Airbus A350-1000 planes, with about 150 premium seats and 161 seats in economy.

"Twenty years ago, 90% of the seats were main cabin," said Ekrem Dimbiloglu, Delta's managing director for onboard strategy and experience, adding that the share of premium seats could soon represent as much as 70% on some Delta flights.

In October, British Airways announced that the top level of the two-tier A380 would be entirely composed of premium seats. Then this month, Singapore Airlines revealed that it is investing €1.4 billion to upgrade its luxury long-haul cabins – including the largest double bed in commercial aviation in first class.

Some airlines already offer services without any economy seats, such as all-business class carriers BeOnd and La Compagnie, while Jet2 recently announced a new charter service which will use a specially configured Boeing 737-800NG with 76 business class seats.

A rise in premium amenities

Consultancy Cirium estimates that premium seats among the 42 carriers in the three major airline alliances (SkyTeam, Oneworld and Star Alliance) and Middle East carriers now represent 19% of total volume compared with 17.1% in 2019.

Other new options include giving customers choice among meal options prior to boarding and free wifi. There have also been a slew of announcements of new and beautified airport lounges, including by Southwest Airlines, which was once known as a discount carrier.

But the increasing tendency of airlines to market to customers who can afford premium amenities could open the door to a discount carrier, although higher fuel costs have added to the challenges facing all airlines.

A joint EU team will be present at the peace talks in Abu Dhabi, together with France, Germany and the UK. The possibility of engaging directly with the Russians, never done before, remains on the table.

The European Commission and the European Council will send a joint team of senior officials to the round of trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi that the United States will host between Ukraine and Russia.

The negotiations will unfold over two days: 10 and 11 November.

"The EU will be present alongside our partners," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday morning after speaking with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"Freedom of navigation in the Black Sea must be restored and preserved. I reiterated my support for his (Zelenskyy's) call for a ceasefire covering food and energy infrastructure."

A spokesperson for the European Council also confirmed the participation.

The institutions will be joined by the E3: France, Germany and the United Kingdom.

The EU team will be led by Bjoern Seibert, von der Leyen's chief of cabinet, and Anna-Maria Boura, chief foreign policy advisor to European Council President António Costa.

Both institutions previously indicated their willingness to engage directly with the Russian delegation, something that has never happened in the context of the peace talks.

At this stage, however, it is not clear if this face-to-face will happen.

Jared Kushner, the US special envoy, said last week that the multilateral format would be organised "if progress is made", though he did not say whether this would be in Abu Dhabi or elsewhere at a later date.

Kushner's long social media post laying down principles to reframe Europe's security architecture after the war has triggered pushback among allies, with Zelenskyy calling it "dangerous". European officials believe the discussion is premature and misguided given that Russia is yet to make a single concession at the negotiating table.

The confirmation of the EU team comes after Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent a scathing letter to Costa complaining about the "disarray" in diplomatic formats and demanding the appointment of a special European envoy.

In his reply, Costa agreed to put the issue on the table at this week's informal summit in Dublin, Ireland, which will take place right after the Abu Dhabi meeting.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski agreed with Meloni and warned that Eastern European's interests should be considered.

"The last thing we want is Western Europe dealing with Russia, over the heads of the East Europeans," Sikorski said from Warsaw.

The Abu Dhabi talks will mark the resumption of trilateral peace negotiations since February, when the war on Iran abruptly shifted Washington's focus.

The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, together with Kyrylo Budanov and Sergiy Kyslytsya, head and deputy head of the president's office; and Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the ruling party in the Parliament.

The Russian delegation will be headed by Vladimir Medinsky, aide to President Vladimir Putin, and Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin.

The US will be represented by special envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner.

The European Commission’s entrance exam, EPSO, is starting between November 9 and November 13. But over half of this year's applicants are Italian, which clashes with an internal hiring rule forcing departments to prioritise candidates from underrepresented countries.

The EU's permanent civil service suffers from severe geographical imbalances. Germany and France sit at just 64% and 73% of their targeted staffing benchmarks, while a retirement wave is set to empty 16% of all active German official posts.

To correct this, the Commission enacted a 2025 internal HR framework prioritising 15 "underrepresented" member states in the upcoming hiring processes. The mandate legally forces managers to invite at least one candidate from these countries to final job interviews. This will apply to candidates who pass this year's EPSO generalist exam and enter the EU jobs reserve list.

But 2026's registration came with a record-breaking statistical difference. Out of roughly 175,000 total applicants, nearly 80.000 were from Italy.

Because the exam is a blind, merit-based test of raw scores, this means Italian candidates (and a broader surge from Southern Europe) are mathematically positioned to sweep the final hiring lists, while youth in Northern and Western Europe are largely ignoring the call.

How can the Commission ensure both fairness and representation? Will the future generations of Eurocrats be overwhelmingly Italian? Our poll is anonymous and takes only a few seconds to complete. The results will be featured across XL's EU-wide coverage, including videos, articles and newsletters, and will help shape our reporting as we examine how Europe can secure its position in the age of artificial intelligence.

The US president expressed confidence that a peace agreement between Kyiv and Moscow was within reach, despite deep divisions over territorial concessions and post-war security guarantees.

US President Donald Trump suggested that Ukraine's territory could change as part of a future agreement with Russia, days before US-mediated talks between Kyiv and Moscow in Abu Dhabi.

"I think we're going to have it done and I think it's going to happen, and they're going to end up with a little bit different shape (for) Ukraine," Trump told CBS's "60 Minutes" in an interview published on Monday.

His remarks come ahead of trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the US, scheduled for 10–11 November in Abu Dhabi, the UAE.

Trump expressed confidence that an agreement was within reach, although Kyiv and Moscow remain deeply divided over territorial concessions and the security arrangements that would follow any ceasefire.

"There's a very important meeting taking place," Trump said. "I believe that that war is going to end and it's going to end soon. And the only reason it's going to end is because of me."

The US president did not elaborate on what he meant by Ukraine having a different shape or specify which territorial changes he envisaged.

Rubio points to progress on security guarantees

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that progress had been made in discussions over post-war security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe, suggesting that further advances could follow this week's negotiations.

Speaking ahead of a visit to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, Rubio said a central question was what security arrangements would be needed to protect Ukraine and the wider European continent after the war.

"What is the postwar security infrastructure of Ukraine and more broadly of the European continent going to look like?" Rubio told reporters.

"I think that's what the president's alluding to - is that there's been some advances made in what that architecture could look like post-conflict," he added.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that the EU would also be present in Abu Dhabi alongside its partners.

France will also be represented at the negotiations, according to Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot.

Territorial disputes remain a major obstacle

Russia and Ukraine remain far apart over the terms of a potential settlement, particularly the future of Ukrainian territories occupied by Moscow's forces.

Vladimir Putin has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine withdraw its troops from four regions that Moscow illegally claimed to annex in 2022, despite never establishing full control over them.

The Kremlin also insisted that Kyiv abandon its ambitions to join NATO and accept restrictions on the size and capabilities of its armed forces.

Ukraine categorically rejected the demands to cede territory, including areas Russia has failed to capture militarily, and insists that credible security guarantees are essential to prevent another Russian invasion.

Kyiv called for an immediate ceasefire as a first step towards a broader settlement, maintaining that territorial questions would ultimately require direct talks between Zelenskyy and Putin.

Asked about the biggest obstacle to reaching an agreement, Trump pointed to the relationship between the two leaders.

"It was the hatred between Zelensky and Putin," he said.

When asked whether Zelenskyy's hostility towards Putin was understandable given Russia's invasion, Trump referred to what he described as disrespect towards Moscow during an earlier meeting between the two presidents.

Asked whether he trusted Putin or Zelenskyy more, Trump declined to choose.

"I'd rather not say, but I get along with both," he said, adding that he did not believe Putin was deliberately prolonging negotiations.

A physicist has distilled time travel into three lines of proof that shows if spacetime can be sliced into layers of light, every traveller must cross them in the same direction, so no journey can ever loop backwards.

A question many of us have posed in our minds is where would you go if you had a time machine?

Would you head for the year 3000 to see what has become of the human race? Or would you crank the dial backwards like Marty McFly and risk sabotaging your own future? Before you start packing, a physicist has some news that may ruin a few Marvel movies: you may only be able to go one way, and it isn't backwards.

Hongsheng Zhang, a researcher at the University of Jinan in China, has shown that in a broad class of theoretical universes, travelling into your own past is impossible.

The whole argument rests on one fact: "light can never point sideways to a traveller's direction in time," Zhang says.

Imagine spacetime sliced into layers that light itself can travel along. Anything moving slower than light must cross these surfaces in the same direction, like climbing a staircase that never lets you step down.

If you can only ever go up, you can never arrive back on the step where you started.

"My paper asks a narrower question: when does a spacetime permit such a loop, and when does the geometry itself forbid one?" Zhang told Euronews Next.

The two loopholes

Physicists call journeys to the past "closed timelike curves": routes through spacetime that loop back to the very place and moment they began.

"Suppose you wanted to shake hands with your younger self," Zhang says. "To do that you would need a path through spacetime that loops back on itself without ever exceeding the speed of light."

Einstein's equations allow such paths in a handful of scenarios, such as near the core of a spinning black hole.

Crucially, Zhang's research, which has been submitted for peer review, also reveals exactly how a time machine could get around it, and there are only two ways.

The first is twist. Imagine light rays that, instead of travelling side by side, spiral around one another like the strands of a rope. When that happens, the neat surfaces of light can't form, so there is no staircase to keep you climbing.

This is what happens near the centre of a spinning black hole. Einstein's theory says a spinning mass drags space and time around with it, and close to the black hole's core the drag is so strong that moving "forward in time" is bent into a circle.

A traveller following that circle would see their clock ticking forward in time as normal, yet their journey would arrive back at the moment they set off. Physicist Brandon Carter showed in 1968 that such loops exist inside spinning black holes.

But Zhang stresses that twist alone is not the culprit. "Twist on its own does not create a closed curve. It only blocks my argument," Zhang says. "Twist is everywhere in the universe and, as far as we know, harmless."

The second is the shape of the universe itself. The staircase might be perfectly built, but it could lead around the sides of a building, so the top step leads straight back to the bottom, like the impossible staircases in an Escher drawing. You would keep climbing and still end up where you began. Most of the time machines physicists have designed on paper, including those built from wormholes, rely on this trick.

Physicists call this loophole topology, and Zhang believes it is the one to watch. "The loophole that could matter is topology, and that is exactly the one that looks least likely to arise without deliberate engineering," Zhang says.

Destination: tomorrow

Trips to the future, by contrast, are already well established. Einstein showed that moving very fast, or sitting in strong gravity, slows your clock relative to everyone else's. Astronauts returning from six months aboard the International Space Station are about five thousandths of a second younger than they would otherwise have been, according to the European Space Agency.

Zhang is keen to stress the limits of the work. "This is not a claim that time travel is impossible," Zhang says.

For now, though, you may want to pack for tomorrow rather than yesterday... unless you have the Time Stone, of course.

The Argentine-born filmmaker first gained international recognition for his film 'Gloria' and then won Chile's second Oscar with 2017's 'A Fantastic Woman' - which sparked a debate that helped change the law in Chile, allowing people to legally change their gender.

Acclaimed filmmaker Sebastián Lelio, whose ground-breaking drama Una mujer fantástica (A Fantastic Woman) took home an Oscar and a Silver Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival, died on Friday (6 November) at the age of 52.

His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram, citing health reasons without specifying the cause of death.

“His memory will remain forever among us,” the announcement read. “He was a beautiful person who contributed to Chilean culture in great moments of its history.”

Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.

View this post on Instagram

The Argentine-born filmmaker raised in Chile first gained international recognition for his fourth film, 2013's Gloria, whose lead actor Paulina García received the Silver Bear for Best Actress at the Berlinale.

Then came 2017's A Fantastic Woman, which cemented his international reputation but also broke ground with its portrayal of a transgender woman. It starred trans actress Daniela Vega as a waitress and nightclub singer whose life is torn apart by the death of her boyfriend.

Not only did the film win the Oscar for Best International Feature Film (Chile's second Oscar, following the animated short Bear Story), but it sparked a debate that helped change the law in his native Chile, allowing people to legally change their gender.

Lelio’s other films include the queer love story Disobedience, starring Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams; the English-language remake of Gloria, titled Gloria Bell, starring Julianne Moore; and The Wonder – the stunning adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel starring Florence Pugh. It was one of Euronews Culture's favourite films of 2022.

Lelio had begun filming Poeta Chileno (Chilean Poet), based on the book by Alejandro Zambra, in September.

His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.

RIP Sebastián Lelio 1974 - 2026

Three rescue operations were conducted by the Hellenic Coast Guard and Frontex in the early hours of Monday off the Greek coast to rescue 18 people from a boat carrying migrants, while 20 died over the weekend.

At least 20 people were found dead in two boats carrying foreign nationals, about 15 nautical miles south-southwest of Kaloi Limenes, a town in the south of Crete. At the same time, the competent authorities have been mobilised, as three separate search and rescue operations have been carried out, during which a total of 105 people were recovered, including 40 on these two boats.

The boat and those on board were initially located by a container ship sailing under the Moroccan flag, which took part in the operation following coordination by the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre (JRCC), according to the Hellenic Coast Guard.

The Coast Guard rescued 18 foreign nationals from the vessel. During the operation, officers also located and recovered twelve bodies from the boat.

Two more incidents involving migrants

At the same time, two other rescue operations were carried out in the wider sea area south of Crete, under the coordination of the JRCC and with the assistance of the European Border and Frontex.

Specifically, a Frontex unmanned aircraft located a second boat carrying about 40 foreign nationals, at a distance of 31 nautical miles southeast of Crete. They were picked up by a vessel of the European force and are expected to be taken to the port of Kaloi Limenes in Crete.

A similar operation followed for a third boat, which was spotted by a Frontex aircraft about 30 nautical miles south of Kaloi Limenes. Some 47 foreign nationals were on board, who were rescued by a ship of the European force and are also expected to be brought to the southern town of Crete.

Based on the information available so far, a total of about 105 people were rescued in the three operations, while twelve deaths were recorded. Weather conditions in the sea area are described as good.

Deadly weekend

On Friday afternoon, the port authorities received a report of a boat with foreign nationals that was in serious difficulty at sea, about six nautical miles southwest of Kaloi Limenes.

The tug "Pyrrhos" was immediately mobilised, located the vessel and took on board 28 Sudanese nationals, as well as the body of a man.

According to the survivors' statements, two more people on board had fallen into the sea and were missing, which led to a further mobilisation of the authorities.

However, the particularly bad weather conditions, with northerly winds, made both the attempt to tow the boat and the continuation of the recovery operation extremely dangerous.

The vessel was located again in the early hours of the morning, when it was found that there were seven more bodies inside. The boat was then taken to Kaloi Limenes.

In connection with the case, the authorities arrested two Sudanese nationals, aged 28 and 16, who were identified by the other passengers as the individuals allegedly in charge of the smuggling operation. They have been charged with illegal entry into the country, facilitating illegal entry, forming a criminal organisation and fatal exposure.

Crete has become one of the main entry points into the EU for migrants departing from Libya and attempting the dangerous crossing to Greece. Many of the attempted crossings turn deadly when the vessels sink or run into trouble.

Johnny Depp plays Scrooge in a new Dickens adaptation, Irish rockers U2 mark their 50th anniversary, and London's Saatchi Gallery unveils a huge new street art exhibition. Here's what to look out for this week.

Christmas is still over 6 weeks away, but the festive releases are already starting to defrost with Ebenezer, Ti West's new "A Christmas Carol" adaptation.

Meanwhile, for U2 fans Christmas has come early as the band release their 16th studio album, 'Carnaval De Luz', with an upcoming studio tour to follow.

We're also being treated to the opening of two new landmark exhibitions on the history of street art and Brussels' turn-of-the-20th-century art, in London and Paris respectively.

Other added bonuses not mentioned below include 'Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism' at the Ateneum Art Museum in Finland and a doggy-friendly exhibition on dachshunds at The Kunsthalle Bremen in Germany.

Finally, if the darker days are getting you down, part 2 of hit series Rivals is the perfect antidote: pure '80s pomp and scandal that will take your mind off the impending list of presents to buy.

Exhibitions

Bruxelles 1900

When: 10 November 2026 - 25 April 2027

Where: Petit Palais (Paris, France)

In around 1893, architect Victor Horta built the Hôtel Tassel (Tassel House) — a masterpiece of design that marked the foundation of Art Nouveau. It's an aesthetic that quickly spread all across Europe, but its first flourishes in Brussels are a key focus of the Petit Palais' new Bruxelles 1900 exhibition. Featuring over 250 works on display, it also highlights Art Deco, comics, illustration and photography; all of the artistic mediums and movements that defined the city's vibrant and influential turn-of-the-20th-century art scene.

Beyond the Streets

When: 11 November 2026 - 5 May 2027

Where: Saatchi Gallery (London, UK)

As far back as ancient Egypt, versions of street art have always existed. The medium as we know it today of urban graffiti, however, took off in '60s and '70s New York and Philadelphia, while artists like Gérard Złotykamień contributed to its rise across Europe. The Saatchi Gallery is digging into this storied history with one of the biggest and most diverse exhibitions on international street culture, bringing together over 100 creators and spanning six decades. Highlights include a large-scale recreation of a graffitied New York subway carriage, a spray paint infinity room and various hip-hop ephemera. Find out more here.

Bonus highlight: Artist Mire Lee has transformed Oude Kerk, Amsterdam's oldest church, into a striking kinetic art installation with steel and slimy-looking silicone. It’s open from 13 November.

Movies

Ebenezer

Where: Cinemas

When: 13 November

Charles Dickens' 'A Christmas Carol' is a staple of the festive season and has spawned hundreds of on-screen adaptations. Everyone has their favourite (author note: I vote for The Muppet's version) but still, new ones keep coming and the latest is from Ti West, the American director best known for his X trilogy and other works in the horror genre. For this reason, Ebenezer leans into the story's darker, gothic elements in a Tim Burton-esque way, with Johnny Depp playing the titular lead, Rupert Grint (Happy Potter) as Bob Cratchit, and Ian McKellen (The Lord of the Rings) as Marley. It's family-friendly fantasy that signals we've truly entered the countdown to Christmas!

Bonus highlights: Last week was a big week for movie releases, with Oscars favourite Wild Horse Nine and Sylvestor Stallone biopic I Play Rocky hitting the big screen. Fans of city-destroying reptiles should also catch Godzilla Minus Zero.

TV series

Rivals (season 2 part 2)

Where: Disney+

When: 11 November

The salacious 80s melodrama of Rivals is back for part 2 of its second season. Based on a 1988 novel of the same name by Jilly Cooper, it follows a rivalry between a former Olympian/ Tory politician (Rupert Campbell-Black) and a former TV mogul (David Tennant), whose fight for control over a TV empire becomes an allegory for the decade's debauchery. The upcoming episodes take things to their climax, with drama escalating and character's psyches unravelling in the aftermath of a fatal car crash. It will also see the story depart from its original source material, setting things up for a now-greenlit third season.

Bonus highlight: David Thelis stars as the legendary literary detective in Sherlock & Daughter, a new HBO adaptation that's streaming now.

Music

U2: Carnaval De Luz

When: 13 November

After an almost ten year hiatus, Irish rockers U2 are back with their 16th studio album: 'Carnaval de Luz'. It marks 50 years since the band first formed in Dublin, with an eclectic 12-track collection that's fittingly reflective, matured, and at times existential. There's also a notable collaboration with the late country queen Dolly Parton, whose duet on 'torn' ended up being her final ever recording. Another highlight includes 'The Mirror Maker', a song written entirely about the Spanish singer Rosalía which, according to producer Jacknife Lee, took nearly 200 takes to get right. But eventually they found what they were looking for — hopefully fans will too.

Bonus highlight: For a less mainstream vibe, California indie band Wavves are releasing their 11th studio album, 'Cherry Soda', on 13 November 2026.

Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Argentina, on Sunday 8 November, for the first papal visit to the country in nearly 40 years. President Javier Milei welcomed him at Buenos Aires airport, while the city's iconic obelisk was illuminated in his honour.

Argentine President Javier Milei welcomed Pope Leo XIV at Jorge Newbery Airport, where the two leaders shook hands before standing side by side on a red carpet for an official ceremony featuring the national guard. The pope also greeted Karina Milei, the president's sister and secretary general of the presidency, Argentina's senior clergy and a group of children and young people on the tarmac.

That night the Obelisco was illuminated with a projection of the pontiff's face, the first switch-on in a city-wide illumination of monuments and façades, from the Floralis Genérica and Planetario to the Teatro Colón and Cabildo, dressed in Vatican yellow and white.

The four-day visit, the first papal trip to Argentina since John Paul II in 1987, is the second leg of a 12-day tour that began in Uruguay and ends in Peru. It resonates because Argentina is the homeland of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who never returned during his 12-year papacy.

The meeting with Milei, whose austerity has reshaped the economy, produced a pointed contrast: the pope said "the economy must serve the person, not the person."

It's no secret that Germany loves dachshunds.

Initially bred some time around the late 17th century for hunting badgers, the sausage dogs have since been adopted across the world; beloved for their charismatically long bodies, stumpy little legs and sweet, docile nature.

This has also made them a frequent source of inspiration for artists including David Hockney and Andy Warhol, whose dachshund companions became a catalyst for creativity throughout their careers.

The Kunsthalle Bremen explores this in what is the first ever exhibition to be entirely dedicated to the breed, featuring roughly 120 objects and works of art by everyone from Pablo Picasso to Otto Dix.

The space has also been specially designed for its muses, welcoming dachshunds (and other small doggy visitors) with scented surroundings and a dedicated lounge.

As the physician Hippocrates once wrote, "Life is short, and art long".

'The Dachshund: An Icon off the Leash' is open until the 28 March 2027 at the Kunsthalle Bremen.

Good morning. This is Luca Bertuzzi, steering the newsletter this week. In this edition: Europe fights for a seat at the Ukraine peace table, Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming a government, Poland mourns the deadly Kraków attack and von der Leyen heads to the Black Sea.

Save me a seat. Europeans want to make sure they have a say in ending Russia’s war against Ukraine, and the clock is ticking. Foreign ministers gather in Paris on Monday and Tuesday for a G7 meeting, just days before US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv open in Abu Dhabi.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday that Europeans would be “well represented” at the Abu Dhabi discussions and that France would take part, though he did not say who would go or in what capacity.

The talks, scheduled for 10–11 November, are expected to bring together Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations to discuss a potential ceasefire and the security arrangements that could accompany an end to the war.

The G7 ministers meet under France’s presidency, with support for Ukraine high on the agenda: military capabilities, financial assistance and energy support, alongside the Middle East and other crises.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is expected to join on Tuesday for a dedicated session on support for Kyiv and in preparation for the Abu Dhabi talks.

For the Europeans, the central aspect is to defend not only Ukraine but also European security in the negotiations, after US President Donald Trump has touted a major agreement involving Ukraine and potentially all of Europe, without offering details.

From today until 22 November, the Franco-British-led coalition of the willing is conducting a military exercise in Poland, involving 2,800 troops from 11 countries, a crucial test to showcase its credibility and preparation to put in place security guarantees in a post-War Ukraine.

On Monday, France will also host a donor conference with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and Ukrainian authorities to raise funds to repair the damaged Chernobyl containment structure.

Behind the diplomatic flurry lies a growing fear in European capitals that decisions on the continent’s security could be taken without them. Last week, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called for a more coordinated European approach and a clear mandate for who will represent the EU in the talks.

European Council President António Costa has agreed to put EU representation in the peace talks on the agenda of the informal EU leaders’ meeting in Dublin on Friday.

An anti-Bibi coalition. Netanyahu's grip on power is being tested as Eisenkot gets his first chance to form government, Sasha Vakulina reports.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Sunday tasked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country's next government, giving the former military chief the first opportunity to replace Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister.

The decision follows the 27 October election, which left neither bloc with a parliamentary majority. Eisenkot has 28 days to assemble a coalition, with a possible two-week extension, Sasha writes.

Arab-led parties, which secured a record 19 seats amid high voter turnout, could prove decisive. Ra'am has backed Eisenkot, while the Joint List has offered to support him from outside the coalition in an effort to end Netanyahu's long hold on power.

But negotiations are expected to be difficult, with some of Eisenkot's potential coalition partners opposed to relying on Arab-led parties, and deep disagreements remaining over Israel's wars and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.

Poland mourns deadly Kraków shooting. European leaders have voiced solidarity with Poland after a shooting in the southern city of Kraków left six people dead and 16 injured, with EU flags flown at half-mast in tribute to the victims.

A gunman opened fire in Kraków’s historic Main Market Square on Saturday, killing six people and injuring 16, including two police officers. The suspect, a 24-year-old Polish man, was shot by police and arrested. He remains in critical condition.

Polish authorities said preliminary findings suggested far-right ideology may have driven the suspect, though investigators have yet to establish the precise motive. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has called the shooting a terrorist attack, and investigations are ongoing.

Jacek Siewiera, the former head of Poland's National Security Council, told Euronews that it was a huge success that the country managed to avoid terrorist attacks for the past three decades, but the security apparatus fell short in this case.

The attack has drawn messages of solidarity from European leaders including French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Meloni.

Poland has declared two days of national mourning, on Sunday and Monday.

Europe's bleak sea security. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen travels to Romania and Bulgaria to discuss Black Sea security, as Russian drone attacks on commercial shipping raise fears for the safety of maritime traffic and critical infrastructure.

She will meet Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Prime Minister Luca Niculescu in Bucharest on Monday, then head to Bulgaria on Tuesday for talks with Prime Minister Rumen Radev and a visit to the Nikola Vaptsarov Naval Academy in Varna.

The trip comes as Russia’s war spills into the Black Sea. Recent drone attacks have exposed how vulnerable maritime infrastructure and shipping routes are close to EU and NATO territory.

One proposal on the table is a Black Sea maritime security hub to improve surveillance, information-sharing and the protection of critical infrastructure. Romania and the Commission have already discussed phasing it in, with the aim of complementing NATO’s military activities in the region.

Russian strikes on Ukraine leave 850,000 without power as Zelenskyy reports drone attack on Komyshuvakha

Zelenskyy said Russia had launched a drone strike on the site of a recent attack on Komyshuvakha, where rescuers have been carrying out search operations following a bombing that killed at least 55 people on Monday.

Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight reportedly left more than 850,000 people without power across the country.

Ukrainian energy firm DTEK said Russian forces had launched a "massive attack" on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting key facilities in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.

"Over 600,000 residents of the region in the Pavlohrad, Samar, Kamianske and Dnipro districts, as well as in the city of Dnipro itself, have been left without power," the company said. Power is gradually being restored in the region, authorities later announced.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy added that there were widespread power outages across the nation, including in Kharkiv Oblast in the northeast and the Zhytomyr region in the northwest, where he said 140 apartment buildings were without heating following a Russian strike.

The 2026 Commission’s entrance exam drew nearly 175,000 applicants, 80,000 from Italy alone. How can the EU address recruitment imbalances while selecting candidates on merit? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot.

EPSO Candidates who applied before March 10 can take the AD5 Generalist Competition test between November 9 and 13.

This round attracted a record 174,727 applicants, far exceeding the roughly 22,000 who applied in the 2019 AD5 competition. It drew particular attention because 79,343 applicants (45.4%) were from Italy, far more than from Spain (13,789), Germany (11,699) and France (10,939). Denmark submitted only 987 applications, and Luxembourg 630.

These figures highlight how popular EU careers are in some countries but not in others.

EU institutions have struggled for decades with the overrepresentation of certain nationalities, leading to a geographical imbalance in Europe’s permanent civil service. This is largely driven by low wages and poor labour market conditions in countries such as Italy, Spain, Greece and Portugal, prompting people to seek better opportunities through EU careers.

Rules require EU institutions to recruit staff from the widest possible range of nationalities, but they struggle to attract staff from parts of Northern and Western Europe. The Commission itself reports that 15 of 27 nationalities are underrepresented, including the Netherlands, Austria, Finland, Sweden, Slovakia and Czechia.

In 2025, the European Commission introduced new recruitment guidelines. Offices must interview at least one candidate from an underrepresented nationality for each post, give them preference if qualifications are the same, and can set nationality-based targets, but must not reserve posts for nationals of a specific member state.

In 2022-2023, Brussels used Joint Action Plans to address geographical imbalances, keeping merit the primary hiring criterion while targeting outreach, candidate support, and vacancy visibility in underrepresented member states. No jobs were reserved for nationals of specific states.

US President Donald Trump said he would possibly meet with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China to discuss "denuclearisation" and how to end the Iran war.

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping might meet in China for trilateral talks next week to discuss the ending of the Iran war.

Trump told reporters he expected to meet Russian and Chinese leaders at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen, China, scheduled for November 18-19.

"Well, I'm going to be going to China," Trump said on Sunday, "and one of the meetings I think will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that'll be interesting."

He added: "We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearisation, but we'll be talking about a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran."

If it happens, it would be historic, although the three leaders are unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests are at odds. This one-of-a-kind trilateral meeting has been acknowledged by the Kremlin on 21 October, saying it was "being prepared."

This followed a Wall Street Journal report that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal in Ukraine that would be favourable to Moscow, which invaded Ukraine in 2022.

"I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content," said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center. "China wants the image but not the costs."

'A diplomatic coup' for Putin

In the US, Trump is often criticised for having a penchant for authoritarian leaders like those of China and Russia, among others.

"Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral, and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup," said Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official who served in former President Barack Obama’s administration.

Trump, with his "crush on authoritarian strongmen," would love the meeting, though he clearly has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Russel.

Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet Xi for the third time this year, amid a fragile trade truce set to expire in January. Beijing is hosting this year’s leaders' summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the US and Russia.

His willingness to meet with Putin also shows the desire to end Russia's isolation that was triggered by its invasion.

The meeting may amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Putin to be seen next to US and Chinese leaders, said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defence of Democracies.

"But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns," Singleton said. "The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential."

With pensioners worried about cuts and young people unsure they will ever get a pension, company-funded individual schemes have long hovered over Spanish politics. Ahead of the 29N elections, we examine the situation.

The so called Austrian backpack was created in Austria to replace traditional redundancy pay and build up a safety pot. Analysts disagree on whether it would work in Spain. With just a few weeks to go before the general election on 29 November, pensions are once again at the centre of the campaign.

Spain spends around 14,498 million euros a month on contributory Social Security pensions, according to the latest official data for September 2026, an increase of 6.3% on the previous year.

The more than nine and a half million pensioners are closely following the parties' proposals and every mention that might suggest a freeze or cut in these benefits. With an average pension of 1,380 euros (source in Spanish), retirees are watching closely what their future will be in the next legislature, something politicians know very well and use to win the votes of one of the most decisive parts of the population.

Spain's public debt is close to 100% of GDP, more precisely it stood at 99.7%, according to data from August 2026. In other words, 1.75 trillion.

In a country with a population already close to 50 million, an unemployment rate above 10%, where 22.8 million people are in work, earning on average 29,540 euros gross a year, (source in Spanish) workers, and especially young people, wonder whether they will ever receive the benefit they are paying into and whether the system will be able to hold up. In that climate an old economic idea has resurfaced: the Austrian backpack.

A campaign with pensions at its core

Political parties know the immense power of the pensioners' vote and have launched a battle to win those millions of votes that could prove decisive in a set of highly polarised and highly tense elections.

The debate on the sustainability of the system has heated up in recent weeks. The spokesperson for the Partido Popular (PP) in Congress, Ester Muñoz, questioned the viability of the public system, and the Socialist Party (PSOE) and Sumar responded by accusing the PP of wanting to privatise it. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has warned of the "sacrifices" that the leader of the opposition, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, would ask of the population if he were to become the next Spanish prime minister.

The PP leader, however, has promised that if he reaches La Moncloa he will uprate pensions in line with inflation and that "in no case" will he question the public system for these benefits. He has also pledged to "guarantee" the future of pension payments for young people.

The Partido Popular says it believes in a public system and maintains that the only party that has frozen pensions was precisely the PSOE during the Zapatero government.

The clash reflects how sensitive the issue is and the concerns of three groups:

On the one hand, there are the pensioners who fear that their benefits will be frozen or lose purchasing power. On the other side are workers, who see part of their wages cut and paid into a common pot, and wonder whether it will really provide them with a benefit once they retire, doubting that the system will return what they have paid in. Finally, there are the young people who enter a precarious labour market late, with low wages, and expect to retire ever later, with no certainty of receiving a pension.

What is the Austrian backpack?

Its official name is "abfertigung neu" and it works as follows:

Companies pay 1.53% of the worker's gross monthly salary into an individual account, a severance fund. That capital belongs to the employee. The fund tops up the public retirement pension, although it can also be drawn in the event of unemployment or if the worker decides to start a business or become self employed. If the worker dies, the fund is not lost.

In fact, this kind of system is not unique to Austria, Italy has the TFR, which is funded by contributions of 7% of salary. The money follows the worker even if they change employer, which is where the name "backpack" comes from.

This system was introduced in Austria in 2003 to replace traditional redundancy compensation. It is not just a pension fund. In fact, the Austrian backpack does not replace the public pension, as Austria maintains a pay as you go public system, like Spain. The fund was designed as severance pay, and the worker can leave it in their account until retirement in order to supplement their public pension. It is a way of guaranteeing some extra money once they stop working.

Its returns are modest. An Austrian MP from NEOS has said that on average the funds yield around 2%. Austria has approved that, from 2028, workers will be able to choose a model without a capital guarantee and with more equities so they can get more out of their money by taking on risk, or transfer the fund to a pension fund to receive a supplementary income.

What its supporters argue in favour of introducing the Austrian backpack in Spain

Economists from Fedea, José Ignacio Conde Ruiz, Florentino Felgueroso and José Ignacio García Pérez, analysed in 2011 (source in Spanish) how it might be introduced in Spain. Supporters highlight that its portability would make it easier to change jobs without losing rights and that it would create individual savings, a safety net for the worker.

The Bank of Spain defended the idea for years. Pablo Hernández de Cos, governor of the Bank of Spain until 2024, presented it as a possible solution to the long term funding problems of the pension system. In 2023, the bank proposed introducing it using 8,000 million euros of European funds.

Specifically, its proposal was to create a fund in the worker's name into which the company would advance part of the redundancy pay, and that this money could be carried from one job to another in the event of a change. In this way, the employee would receive the accumulated money either when they become unemployed or on retirement.

With this, the Bank of Spain aimed to combat job insecurity and temporary contracts in the labour market, benefit people who change jobs and generate that top up when they reach retirement.

What its critics say: the trade unions, its main opponents

Trade unions such as CC.OO. and UGT argue that it would make dismissal "predictable and financially neutral" for employers, a form of prepaid free dismissal. UGT argues that "it punishes companies that do not dismiss staff, as they have to pay funds into their workforce's accounts month after month, increasing their labour costs, and rewards those that resort more frequently to dismissals, by reducing their cost and ease of financing". They also maintain that this measure "would lead to an increase in the number of dismissals" and in staff turnover, by removing any deterrent effect from compensation.

There are also sceptical voices among expert economists, who point out that it would be difficult to apply because Social Security cannot do without contributions when it faces a structural deficit.

Employers themselves are not enthusiastic about the measure either, fearing that it would increase labour costs.

KPMG has calculated that with the Austrian rate of 1.53% it would not be more beneficial than the current redundancy pay, and that contributions of more than 5.48% would be needed in the case of fair dismissal and more than 9.04% in the case of unfair dismissal.

The key lies in the differences between Spain and Austria. In the event of dismissal, changing employer or becoming self employed in the latter country, the backpack follows the worker, which means it replaces traditional redundancy compensation.

What the parties say

The PP is looking at including the Austrian backpack model once again in its election programme for the 29 November election, as it did in 2023, and maintains that it would not reform the pension system. PSOE and Sumar have repeatedly warned that the PP intends to privatise the system, something the PP denies.

The economic team of José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero tried to introduce the Austrian backpack concept, but it ultimately did not go ahead. Years later, the PSOE tried to develop something similar with publicly promoted occupational pension funds under José Luis Escrivá at the Social Security ministry. The Socialist Party has included in plans sent to Brussels a variant renamed "mobility and training fund". This fund would allow workers to cash in the amounts accumulated in their favour in cases of unfair dismissal, geographical mobility, to carry out training activities or at the time of retirement.

Far left parties such as Sumar reject it outright, calling it a "free dismissal mechanism" that increases job insecurity for workers. For their part, the far right party Vox views it with suspicion because of the rise in costs it could mean for SMEs, and instead prioritises direct tax cuts.

The Austrian backpack would not by itself solve the demographic challenge facing the Spanish system and is not a substitute for the public pension. The analyses consulted suggest that its impact in Spain would depend on the percentage contributed, who pays for it and how Social Security is compensated for the contributions it would no longer receive.

A Democratic ‘blue tsunami’ sparked one of the year’s sharpest rotations in Europe: banks rallied, chips sank on data-centre fears.

When Americans voted last week, European investors were watching one question above all: how much room would Donald Trump have left to govern?

By Wednesday morning, they had their answer.

Democrats took control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, a clear defeat for the US president halfway through his term.

On trading floors, the result quickly earned a name: the "blue tsunami".

At first glance, Europe's stock market barely reacted. The Stoxx 600 jumped 1.8% on Wednesday, then gave most of it back. By Friday's close it stood just 0.4% above Tuesday's level.

The Euro Stoxx 50, which tracks the euro area's 50 largest companies, followed the same path. It rose 2% on Wednesday and ended the week just 0.4% higher.

Look beneath the surface, though, and it was one of the most violent reshuffles of the year.

Banks up, tech down

The rotation was clearest at sector level.

European banks rose 3.2% between Tuesday and Friday, with most of the gain on Wednesday alone. Jordi Visser, head of AI macro research at 22V Research, said it was the sector's best week since June.

Travel and leisure stocks did even better, climbing 3.9% as oil prices fell. Brent crude dropped more than 9% on Wednesday, as traders bet that a weakened president would be less likely to escalate the war with Iran.

Utilities gained 2.5% and healthcare 2%. On the other side, energy stocks fell 4.2% on cheaper oil, and technology lost 3.6%.

Europe held up better than Wall Street for a simple reason: its market owns far fewer AI stocks and far more banks.

"The equity market is a distorted mirror of the economy," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, said in a report.

According to Bell, financial companies make up more than 30% of Stoxx 600 earnings, but only 10% of euro area economic activity. After the midterm tech sell-off, European stocks have now pulled ahead of US equities this year in local-currency terms, according to Goldman Sachs.

"European indices are less exposed to the semiconductor correction," Intesa Sanpaolo's equity strategy team said in a report on Friday. The team added that banks were recovering thanks to solid quarterly results.

Thursday's tech blow-up

Most of the damage in tech came in a single session.

The trigger for Thursday's sell-off was not Congress. It was what happened in the states.

Democrats won governors' races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. In all three states, Republican governors had courted the data-centre boom with tax breaks and fast-track permits. The upset in Texas, home to some of the largest AI data-centre projects in the US, hit hardest.

At the same time, voters in parts of Ohio, Illinois, Maine and Florida approved local measures to ban or restrict new data centres.

"The fear of Democrat-inspired opposition to data centres has gained greater political weight, and the risk concerns not only new regulations but above all permits, energy consumption and local resistance," Gian Marco Salcioli, head of global markets strategy at Intesa Sanpaolo, said in the report.

If new governors slow approvals, fewer data centres get built. That means fewer chips, fewer machines to make those chips and less equipment to power them.

European technology stocks fell 3.2% on Thursday alone.

Why bond yields fell

Bonds rallied across the board.

Germany's 10-year Bund yield fell from 3.33% on Tuesday to 3.25% on Friday, after touching its lowest level since late August. France's 10-year yield fell further, from 4.95% to 4.77%. The US 10-year Treasury yield dropped from 4.97% to 4.86%.

According to Peter Williams, economist at 22V Research, bond markets see "greater-than-expected constraints on the war, tariffs, and the artificial intelligence (AI) boom as modestly disinflationary shifts over the medium term."

The AI part matters for borrowing too.

To pay for their data centres, the big US cloud companies, known as hyperscalers, have become some of the world's largest borrowers, and they compete with governments for the same investors.

Last week alone, Meta sold $10 billion (€9 billion) of bonds in its first euro-denominated deal. The sale drew more than $59 billion (€53 billion) of orders, a record for a corporate issuer in Europe.

"The market continues to finance the investment programmes of the big hyperscalers, but demands increasingly higher compensation," Intesa Sanpaolo credit strategist Pasquale Lodato said.

A pause in data centres would flip that. Less AI spending would mean less Big Tech debt, and less competition for governments funding their deficits.

Here is how the Euro Stoxx 50 ended the week, from Tuesday's close to Friday's close.

Europe's five biggest winners after the midterms

5. Saint-Gobain: +5.4%

The French building materials group rode the rotation. Construction stocks benefit from lower borrowing costs, and they were among Europe's best-performing sectors on Wednesday.

4. BBVA: +5.7%

The Spanish lender led the rally in European banks, which rose more than 4% on Wednesday alone. The sector has now largely recovered from its weakness in September and October. Markets are refocusing on earnings that mostly beat expectations.

3. Prosus: +6.5%

The biggest asset of this Dutch tech investor is a large stake in Chinese tech giant Tencent. Prosus gained as investors swapped US AI exposure for Chinese technology. Tencent and Alibaba both jumped more than 6% in Hong Kong on Thursday.

2. Bayer: +7.2%

The German drugs and crop science group rose 4.6% on Wednesday. Bank of America analysts said that, with most of its legal battles behind it, Bayer had a path to stronger cash generation and lower debt. Healthcare was also one of the week's favoured defensive sectors.

1. Adyen: +8.9%

The Dutch payments group was among the biggest beneficiaries of money leaving AI. Its shares had fallen sharply after results in late October, when it cut its profit margin target to fund more investment, and were down about 35% this year. On Friday, Citi analysts said the market was too focused on the short-term hit to margins and was underestimating the company's long-term growth.

Europe's five biggest losers after the midterms

5. ASML: −7.3%

Europe's most valuable company is the only maker of the most advanced chipmaking machines. It fell 6.5% on Thursday. Fewer data centres mean fewer new chip factories, and fewer orders for ASML's machines.

4. Nokia: −8.7%

The Finnish network equipment maker has been repositioning itself around AI networking. It fell 7.5% on Thursday as investors questioned how many new data centres would need its equipment.

3. Siemens Energy: −9.0%

The German maker of gas turbines and grid equipment fell 8% on Wednesday. Much of its recent growth has come from turbines that power US data centres, and Texas was one of its key markets.

2. Infineon: −12.7%

Europe's largest chipmaker is a major supplier of power chips for data centres. It fell 8.5% on Thursday alone and reports results on Tuesday.

1. Rheinmetall: −19.1%

Germany's largest defence group had its worst week of the year. Investors first questioned whether a Democratic Congress would back the scale of military spending the Trump administration wants.

Then on Thursday the company cut its 2026 sales forecast for the second time in three months. It said it no longer expected a contract for its Boxer armoured vehicle programme this year, and the shares fell 16% that day.
